forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

summary.summary: Covering report bringing Folkestone & Hythe's 2025-26 Annual Governance Statement to committee for approval, together with a 2026-27 improvement action plan and end-of-year updates on last year's actions. The statement was prepared under the CIPFA 2016 framework and its May 2025 addendum, and has been reviewed by the statutory officers, the Head of the East Kent Audit Partnership and external auditor Grant Thornton; the report's own risk table rates every identified risk as low likelihood. No governance failures, financial figures or distress language appear in the covering report — the AGS itself and its action plans are separate appendices not included in this document.

news_drafts.headline: Folkestone and Hythe's underlying need to borrow rose £15.8m to £172.6m in 2025/26, driven by housing and Otterpool Park
news_drafts.lead:
Folkestone and Hythe District Council's capital financing requirement (CFR), the total it has spent on long-lasting assets that it has not yet paid for, rose by £15.8m in 2025/26 to £172.6m, from £156.8m a year earlier. The figure is in the treasury management annual report going to the council's Cabinet on 14 October 2026.

The report attributes the rise to capital spending, meaning money spent on things that last, during the year. That included £9.3m on projects in the housing revenue account (the separate, rent-funded account for the council's own homes) and £4.1m on the Otterpool Park Garden Town development. A further £0.8m went on Changing Tides and £0.1m on a waste vehicle.

The council paid for the increase in two ways. It took £10.3m of new external borrowing, which brought its external loans to £117.8m. It also raised its internal borrowing by £5.5m to £54.8m. Internal borrowing means using the council's own cash balances to pay for capital spending instead of taking out a loan. That saves interest but uses up cash the council would otherwise hold. The £54.8m covers 32% of the CFR.

The report describes this as the council's strategy to reduce risk and keep interest costs low, by holding borrowing and investments below their underlying levels.

news_drafts.headline: Folkestone and Hythe projects £504k deficit despite break-even budget as reserves draw down 13.5%
news_drafts.lead: Folkestone and Hythe council is projecting a revenue deficit of £504k for 2026/27, a £503k adverse variance from its budgeted break-even position, according to Q1 budget monitoring reported to its Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee on 29 September. The shortfall emerges despite the council drawing down £3.079m (13.5%) of its reserves to cover service pressures and capital projects. Housing benefits are overspending by £456k, adding to broader service variances totalling £1.438m above budget. The council is responding by increasing its General Fund capital borrowing by £3.4m to £14.554m, and funding an additional £935k of capital expenditure from reserves rather than external finance. Reserves are projected to fall from £22.7m to £19.4m by year-end.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Statement of Account 2025-26 - 24 November 2026 v2
findings.headline: Total usable reserves rose to £63,705k at 31 March 2026 from £53,261k at 31 March 2025
findings.detail: The paper says the council has retained a prudent level of reserve balances to support the MTFS, and that reserves are held to manage future risks. It also notes the council may need to deploy reserves for other important needs in the current financial climate.
findings.matters: A rise in usable reserves in the year, alongside the MTFS funding gap, shows the balance a council holds to cover forecast pressures, which other councils and lenders would compare.
findings.figures: £63,705k total usable reserves at 31 March 2026; £53,261k at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: the Council has retained a prudent level of reserve balances which will support the delivery of the Medium-Term Financial Strategy

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Statement of Account 2025-26 - 24 November 2026 v2
findings.headline: Capital programme financed £5,012k from borrowing, against a latest budget of £3,930k
findings.detail: The paper says the capital programme was financed from a combination of borrowing, grants, capital receipts and revenue contributions. The financing table shows borrowing at £5,012k against a latest budget of £3,930k, a higher figure than budgeted even as total capital spend fell.
findings.matters: Borrowing above budget in a year of underspend shows the council drawing on borrowing where other funding fell short, which is relevant to finance directors and lenders looking at borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £5,012k borrowing funding; £3,930k latest budget for borrowing; £1,082k variance
findings.quote: As can be seen from the table above, the Capital Programme was financed from a combination of borrowing, grants, capital receipts and revenue contributions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Statement of Account 2025-26 - 24 November 2026 v2
findings.headline: Current MTFS forecast shows a cumulative funding gap of £5.4m over its lifetime, with reserves to absorb the deficit over four years
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS, which runs to March 2030, shows a cumulative funding gap of £5.4m. It also says the council has reserves to help mitigate these deficits, but that the reserves will diminish over time as they absorb the deficit over the four-year period.
findings.matters: A forecast gap that reserves are expected to absorb over time is the situation many councils describe, and it shows how the reserve position is expected to change over the MTFS period.
findings.figures: £5.4m cumulative funding gap over the MTFS lifetime; four-year period to March 2030
findings.quote: the current MTFS forecast shows a cumulative funding gap of £5.4m over the lifetime of this MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Statement of Account 2025-26 - 24 November 2026 v2
findings.headline: Draft HRA outturn shows a £3.7m decrease in net expenditure to the HRA Reserve against budget
findings.detail: The paper reports a provisional HRA outturn with income of £20,657k against a budget of £21,099k, and expenditure of £15,485k against a budget of £18,161k. The net effect on the HRA Reserve is shown as a decrease in net expenditure of £3.7m against budget.
findings.matters: A large HRA variance against budget that feeds into the HRA Reserve affects the reserve available for the housing programme, which lenders and other councils with HRA stock would track.
findings.figures: £3.7m decrease in net expenditure to the HRA Reserve; £21,099k latest approved income budget; £20,657k income outturn; £18,161k latest approved expenditure budget; £15,485k expenditure outturn
findings.quote: The table above shows that overall the draft position is a projected decrease in net expenditure to the HRA Reserve of £3.7m for the HRA against budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Statement of Account 2025-26 - 24 November 2026 v2
findings.headline: HRA capital outturn of £17,776k against a latest approved budget of £33,838k, with £13.2m of the variance attributed to new build purchases completing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says the underspend is largely due to delay in completing the purchase of new build units, many of which will now complete in 2026/27. The HRA capital programme table shows a variance of £16,062k against the latest approved budget.
findings.matters: Delayed completion of purchases moves both the spend and the associated borrowing or funding into the next financial year, which matters to any reader tracking HRA capital timing.
findings.figures: £16.1m lower expenditure; £13.2m of new build completions moved to 2026/27; £33,838k latest approved budget; £17,776k final outturn; £16,062k variance
findings.quote: Largely this underspend relates to the delay in completion of the purchase of new build units, many of which will now complete in 2026/27 (£13.2m).
